progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: chem-m7-c03 (homologous series; CnH2n+2; intramolecular covalent bonds against intermolecular dispersion forces; boiling separates molecules without breaking covalent bonds; longer chains have more electrons and more contact, so stronger dispersion forces and higher boiling points; branching lowers boiling point; four reference boiling points: methane −162 °C, butane about −1 °C, octane 126 °C, wax solid). chem-m7-c01 (alkane names to C8). chem-m5-p01 and chem-m6-p02 (validity, reliability and accuracy in plain words; independent, dependent and controlled variables; risk assessment as hazard, harm, control; a logged temperature-time graph). Year 11 (kinetic particle model: temperature as average kinetic energy; evaporation from the surface). Not assumed: evaporative cooling as a method, volatility, secondary data as a term, GHS hazard codes.
progression.startsWith: Choose comparable members and a safe property test. The video opens: Here are three bottles of clear, colourless liquid: heptane, octane and nonane. They're alkane neighbours, and they look identical. The last video said a longer chain means stronger dispersion forces.
progression.stopsAfter: choosing straight-chain members of one series and a property that needs no heating; describing the evaporative cooling method with its variables, controls and repeats; reading the logged runs and the results table; explaining the trend with intramolecular and intermolecular bonding; extending it with published boiling points and describing the shrinking step; judging validity, reliability and accuracy; stating the limits; writing the risk assessment and disposal for heptane, octane and nonane, including why hexane is substituted. No reactions (chem-m7-c04a), no reason for the shrinking step, no alcohols (chem-m7-c05).
progression.nextLesson: what happens when a double bond meets a reagent (chem-m7-c04a, "What can add across a C=C bond?", playlist order 5; see Open decisions on the route's next field).

teaching.task: The last video said a longer chain means stronger dispersion forces. How do you test that safely in a school lab, what do the results show, and how far can you trust them?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) the three liquids look identical, so a claim about forces needs a test (1); (2) straight-chain members of one series differ only by CH₂, so chain length is the single change; a branch changes shape too; methane to butane are gases; pentane boils at 36 °C, so its vapour builds up fastest and it is the biggest fire risk (2); (3) boiling would mean heating a flammable liquid near an ignition source; only the fastest molecules have enough energy to escape, so those left behind are slower on average and the liquid cools; faster evaporation, bigger drop (3); (4) the soaked sleeve starts at the sample's temperature, so the drop comes from evaporation alone; logging until the lowest reading catches the full drop; repeats (4); (5) one independent variable, one dependent, and the controls, including air flow, because moving air speeds up evaporation (5); (6) heptane falls fastest and furthest, then warms once the liquid has gone (6); (7) the means fall with each extra carbon (7); (8) evaporating breaks no covalent bonds, and those bonds are the same kind in every member; each CH₂ adds electrons and contact, so stronger dispersion forces hold the molecules back, fewer escape each second, and the drop is smaller (8); (9) published boiling points reach the members that cannot be tested at room temperature and rise at every step, by a shrinking amount (9); (10) a higher boiling point goes with a smaller drop, so two independent methods agree (10); (11) validity needs chain length as the only change; repeats agree within about half a degree; accuracy means the probe reads true temperatures, checked against a calibrated thermometer; the ranking that matches the data book is agreement, which supports the conclusion but is not accuracy (11); (12) the drop compares evaporation, it is not a boiling point or a force measurement; air flow and the amount of liquid on the paper cause scatter; the conclusion covers straight chains only (12); (13) the hazards and their controls, starting with substitution (hexane left out because repeated exposure can damage nerves), and disposal (13); memory aid (14); attempts and brief feedback (15 to 18); decision rule and handoff (19); key notes (20).
teaching.conversationalApproach: three bottles of heptane, octane and nonane look identical, and the last video claimed that a longer chain means stronger dispersion forces, so the practical asks how to test that claim safely in a school lab and how far the result can be trusted. Straight-chain members of one series are chosen so only chain length changes, liquids rather than gases, with pentane left out as the biggest fire risk. Heating a flammable liquid is ruled out, so the test is evaporative cooling at room temperature: only the fastest molecules escape, the liquid left behind cools, and a faster evaporation gives a bigger temperature drop. The method (filter paper sleeve on a probe, a 30 second soak, logging until the reading stops falling, three trials in a fume cupboard) and the variables are each given a reason, the logged runs and the results table show the drop shrinking with each extra carbon, and the trend is explained by dispersion forces between molecules while no covalent bond breaks. Published boiling points extend the series and agree with the drops; validity, reliability and accuracy are separated (agreement is not accuracy), the limits and the risk assessment follow, with hexane swapped out as a substitution control. The memory aid is longer chain, smaller chill. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Here are three bottles of clear, colourless liquid: heptane, octane and nonane. They're alkane neighbours, and they look identical. The last video said a longer chain means stronger dispersion forces. That's a claim. So how do you test it in a school lab, safely, and how far can you trust what you find?
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "The table shows the normal boiling points of four straight-chain alkenes. Describe the trend in boiling point and explain it with reference to the intramolecular and intermolecular bonding present." Table: but-1-ene −6.3 °C; pent-1-ene 30.0 °C; hex-1-ene 63.5 °C; hept-1-ene 93.6 °C. A new series (alkenes; the scenes use alkanes); tests describing the trend with the shrinking step and the bonding explanation in the syllabus's words. Crossed mistake: "longer chains have stronger covalent bonds" (site card 3 Common error). (A2) "A student plans to find the effect of chain length on volatility by heating pentane, hexane and 2-methylpentane in an open test tube over a Bunsen burner and recording the temperature at which each liquid boils. Evaluate the validity and safety of this plan." Tests both route boundaries (comparable members; a safe property test). The aim names chain length (Revision 3, Codex check 101): branching is a valid variable in a general volatility comparison, so the plan is judged only on whether it can isolate chain length. Answer: not valid for this aim (2-methylpentane is branched, so shape changes as well as chain length, and the effect of length cannot be isolated; use straight chains such as heptane, octane and nonane); not safe (an open flame near highly flammable vapour; pentane boils at 36 °C); improvement: evaporative cooling in a fume cupboard with no flames, or published boiling points. Crossed mistake: "use a smaller flame".
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "conduct an investigation to compare the properties of organic chemical compounds within a homologous series, and explain these differences in terms of bonding (ACSCH035)" "describe the procedures required to safely handle and dispose of organic substances (ACSCH075)" this video prepares students to plan, carry out and evaluate a first-hand comparison within the alkane series, and extends it with the secondary boiling point data that chem-m7-c03 handed over; it does not claim that watching it is conducting it. It teaches: choosing members of one series with straight chains so that chain length is the only change; why heptane, octane and nonane (liquids at room temperature) and not methane to butane (gases), pentane (boils at 36 °C, extremely flammable) or hexane (nerve damage with repeated exposure, so it is substituted); choosing a property that can be measured without heating a flammable liquid: evaporation, measured as the temperature drop of a probe wrapped in a soaked filter-paper sleeve; why evaporation cools (only the fastest molecules escape, so those left behind are slower on average); the method, the variables and the repeats; reading logged temperature-time runs; the results table and means; explaining the trend in terms of bonding (intramolecular covalent bonds unchanged and unbroken; intermolecular dispersion forces stronger with each CH₂, so fewer molecules escape each second); extending the trend with published boiling points for C1 to C9 at 101.3 kPa, with the shrinking step described, not explained; two methods agreeing; validity, reliability and accuracy for this investigation; the limits of the method; the risk assessment and disposal. Not re-taught: why dispersion forces grow with chain length, intramolecular against intermolecular, branching and contact (chem-m7-c03, recalled in one clause each, "as the last video showed"); the meanings of validity, reliability and accuracy (chem-m5-p01; recalled in one clause each and applied). Not here: alkenes and alkynes as subjects of the practical (attempt 1 uses alkene data only to transfer the trend); reactions of hydrocarbons (chem-m7-c04a onward); solubility (chem-m7-c03); a quantitative link between temperature drop and force strength; the reason the boiling point step shrinks (site correction 5 in c03; beyond this course); alcohols (chem-m7-c05).

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key as chem-m7-c03: carbon ink; hydrogens soft grey; main chain pale blue; covalent bonds solid ink; dispersion forces dotted pale-blue flicker lines; plus, for this practical, the three alkanes' runs in three fixed colours (heptane teal, octane amber, nonane violet), used on bottles' label edges, graph lines, table rows and the agreement strip; the temperature readout amber digits; evaporation wisps pale grey with warm-orange energy dots; hazards terracotta, controls green. Board layout (three zones, constant, as chem-m6-p02): top-left the short task line; the centre holds the apparatus or the graph; the right third holds the current card (method step, variables, table, validity card, risk table), one at a time. Clutter rule: at most three bright text items; every label dims when its sentence ends. Reuse: `p03-dropper-bottle-v1.png` (2000 × 2000: a clear glass dropper bottle with a black bulb, clear liquid inside and a blank cream label; no text, no hands), shown three times side by side with coded label text on the blank label ("heptane C₇H₁₆", "octane C₈H₁₈", "nonane C₉H₂₀"); `m7-bromine-water-colourless-v1.png` (2000 × 2000: an open clear test tube about half full of colourless liquid, no label), used here only as a sample tube of colourless liquid with a coded tag under it (the plate shows nothing bromine-specific); `m5x-stopper-v1.png` (a black rubber stopper, placed on the sample tubes in scene 13 by a coded drop); `m5x-safety-glasses-v1.png`, `m5x-gloves-v1.png` (risk table head; gloves tagged "if your school requires"); `m5x-waste-bottle-v1.png` (2000 × 2000: an amber glass jar with a black cap and a blank cream label; coded label "Organic waste"); `m7-camping-gas-burner-v1.png` (scene 2, small, for methane to butane as gases; chem-m7-c03's hook plate). Considered, not used: `m6-ph-probe-holder-v1.png` (inspected: a pH electrode with a blue body in a stand holder; it is not a temperature probe), `c8-thermometer-hot-v1.png` (a glass thermometer: the method needs a logging probe, and a glass bulb wrapped in paper would mislead), `m6-burette-clamp-stand-v1.png` (the stand holds a burette). New plates: `m7-temp-probe-sleeve-stand-v1.png` and `m7-fume-cupboard-v1.png`; see Codex asset brief. No human figures.
